title: 3-Read Friday #69: Atomisation, Teacher Likability, and Classroom Routines
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue #69 of 3-Read Friday opens with Kris Boulton's launch post for his new newsletter, introducing his three-part taxonomy of atomisation -- routine, factual, and conceptual -- which Barton flags as a topic he's long been fascinated by after having Boulton on his podcast. Robert Pondiscio follows with an 'Edu-Homily Watch' entry challenging the popular claim that students won't learn from teachers they don't like, arguing the research shows the causal arrow runs the other way: students come to like teachers who help them learn. Blake Harvard closes by distinguishing a 'simple' classroom -- built on predictable, safe routines -- from an 'easy' one, where students can coast without real thinking, arguing the best defense against an easy classroom is a well-established simple one. Barton frames the issue around routines and relationships: how teaching is structured (atomised routines, classroom routines) and how teachers are perceived (liked because effective, not effective because liked).
points: Boulton's atomisation taxonomy (routine, factual, conceptual) gives Barton -- self-described as long obsessed with the concept -- a more precise vocabulary for a topic he's previously only discussed informally on his podcast.

Pondiscio's research-backed reversal of the 'likability' folk wisdom -- students like teachers they learn from, not the other way around -- directly targets a popular but research-thin claim traceable to Rita Pierson's viral TED Talk.

Harvard's simple-vs-easy classroom distinction gives teachers a diagnostic question for auditing their own routines: are things predictable and safe (simple) without also being low-effort and low-thought (easy)?

Barton's synthesis links all three items to a shared claim: durable, defensible teaching practice comes from structure and evidence (atomised routines, research on likability, predictable classroom routines), not from comfortable folk intuitions.
quotes: Long-time listeners to my podcast will know I am obsessed with Atomisation, largely thanks to Kris Boulton.
Do students learn best from the teachers they like? If the answer is yes, then does that mean teachers should start practising telling jokes, and focus on delivering fun, engaging lessons?
Robert dives into the research, reaching a firm conclusion: Students learn from teachers they like. But they like teachers they learn from.

I love the distinction Blake makes here between a simple classroom, built on routines where things feel predictable and safe, and an easy classroom, where students can get away with doing very little thinking.
The best way to avoid an easy classroom is to start with a simple one.
